newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Body parts, produce, fly in air in Jerusalem carnage.
newsitem.headline: Body parts, produce, fly in air in Jerusalem carnage.

text.p: First mid-day shoppers heard two explosions within seconds of each other. Then they saw body parts and summer fruit and vegetables flying in the air.

An immense fireball and a cloud of smoke engulfed the crowded Mahane Yehuda street market in the heart of Jewish west Jerusalem on Wednesday in the twin blasts, blamed by police on two Arab suicide bombers.
Fourteen people, including the bombers, were killed and more than 150 wounded as the bombs, packed with nails and screws, ripped through the bustling market.
"Peace? Peace? They call this peace?" shrieked a middle-aged Israeli woman in the midst of the carnage and confusion, shaking her hands furiously in the air.
Bits of brain were splattered across the asphalt but it was not clear whether they were human or had been blown out of a neighbouring butcher's shop.
The explosions occurred just as Israel and the Palestinians had been preparing for a U.S. Middle East envoy's mission on Thursday to try to salvage peacemaking from a four-month-long crisis.
"Death to Arabs," "Kill them all", shouted a few dozen Jewish youths who gathered in the market two hours after the explosions.
Police, rescue workers and bystanders struggled to remove the dead and wounded over a mash of blown-up watermelons, eggplants, body parts and blood.
"I went to shop there because it was cheaper," a German Christian missionary, her body covered with burns and eyebrows singed off, told Reuters while attached to a respirator in a Jerusalem hospital.

"I saw suddenly a big bomb and a lot of smoke and fire," said the woman, who declined to be named because she had not been able to contact her family. "The second explosion came right away and I was thrown to the floor.
"It was wonderful because a lot of people helped me immediately...I feel sorry for the people who set up those bombs because they can't be happy people," she said.
Police swiftly closed the market to search through garbage bins and debris for any more bombs.

One man in his early 30s who appeared to be paralysed, a market butcher in his smock and rubber boots, lay on the sidewalk on a stretcher after he was cut off from medical crews by a swarm of pedestrians.
"Why don't they take him? Where is a doctor?" one woman shouted.
A bearded ultra-Orthodox Jew and a journalist picked up the stretcher and plunged into the chaos of rescue crews to find an ambulance. Victims' skin was scorched black.
The blast touched both Jews and Arabs who work side by side in the narrow alleyways of the partly covered market.

"I heard a huge boom. Two seconds later there was a second boom, just as strong if not stronger. There were people all over the ground -- Arabs, Jews. Police came, ambulances. My God," said Samir Salah Daoud Joumhour, a 15-year-old Arab worker.
Bearded ultra-Orthodox Jews collected pieces of scattered flesh and bone for burial as required by religious law.
An ultra-Orthodox Jew named Micha searched his memory for a relevant explanation from the Bible.
"Esau envied Jacob. Ishmael was jealous of Isaac. Arabs hate the Jews, the Jews are God's chosen people, and this is the result," the man said.
